newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodians, not USA, must decide, new premier says.
newsitem.headline: Cambodians, not USA, must decide, new premier says.

text.p: Foreign Minister Ung Huot, the man nominated to replace Cambodia's ousted first prime minister, on Thursday rebuffed a U.S. decision not to recognise his appointment, saying Cambodians had to make their own decisions.

Ung Huot, a senior member of ousted First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party, was on Wednesday chosen by the royalist party to succeed Ranariddh but Washington said there was no evidence the party had elected him on a free and democratic basis.
"Our people have to decide, not America," Ung Huot told reporters when asked about Washington's decision.
Ung Huot, speaking to reporters on his way into a cabinet meeting, said steps were being taken to put an end to human rights abuses in the country.
Second Prime Minister Hun Sen ousted Ranariddh in a bloody coup in July 6. Western officials say up to 40 Cambodians have been killed in the wake of the coup, some of them after being tortured.
The United States said on Wednesday it was "very concerned" by the decision to make Ung Huot the country's co-prime minister and did not recognise him in that position.
"We are very concerned about the decision this morning to make the Cambodian foreign minister co-prime minister with Hun Sen," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told a news briefing.
"We see no evidence whatsoever that FUNCINPEC has met...and has elected on a free basis, on a democratic basis, a successor to Prince Ranariddh," he said.

"We urge the authorities in Phnom Penh to refrain from announcing a new first prime minister until Prince Ranariddh's political party has an opportunity to make a reasoned decision on this matter, free of coercion, free of intimidation."
It was not for Ung Huot to accept the job without Ranariddh expressing an opinion, he said.
The United States suspended aid to Cambodia for 30 days after Ranariddh's ouster.

The U.S. Senate voted 99-0 late on Wednesday to halt U.S. aid to Cambodia until the secretary of state certified that the Cambodian government was established by free and fair elections, and not by force or coup d'etat.

Hun Sen said after Ranariddh's ouster that he wanted the coalition between his Cambodian People's Party (CPP) and FUNCINPEC to remain in place and the royalist party to choose a new first prime minister.

A dissident FUNCINPEC faction which broke with Ranariddh in April and the remnants of the royalist party still in Phnom Penh in the aftermath of Ranariddh's ouster, agreed on Wednesday that Ung Huot should replace the prince as powerful Second Prime Minister Hun Sen's coalition partner.
His nomination will be forwarded to the National Assembly when it opens on July 28.
Burns also said the United States was "very deeply troubled" by reports of killings in the aftermath of Hun Sen's ouster of his co-premier.
As many as 40 of Ranariddh's supporters have been killed since his overthrow and there was evidence some of the victims had been tortured, diplomatic sources in Phnom Penh said.
Ung Huot said Hun Sen was taking measures to end human rights abuses.
"When there is trouble, when there is fighting, we have to expect all this ... but Cambodia should not go through this again," Ung Huot said.
"Hun Sen is taking measures to solve this by sending members of parliament from FUNCINPEC and the CPP to places where there is trouble. Measures are being taken every hour," he said.

FUNCINPEC won a 1993 election supervised by the United Nations but agreed to a coalition with Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party (CPP) after Hun Sen objected to the poll result and the country faced splitting up along factional lines.
